texts.preamble: Badam Sampath Kumar vs The State Of Andhra Pradesh on 11 November, 2019 Author: Cheekati Manavendranath Roy Bench: Cheekati Manavendranath Roy 1 Cmr, J. Crl. P.No.6622 of 2019 Hon'Ble Sri Justice Cheekati Manavendranath Roy Criminal Petition No.6622 of 2019 Order:
texts.facts: This petition is filed under Section 438 Cr.P.C. to enlarge the petitioner on bail in the event of his arrest. The petitioner herein is accused No.1 in Crime No.437 of 2019 of P.M.Palem, Visakhapatnam. The alleged offences against the petitioner herein are under Sections 272, 273, 328 of IPC and Sections 8(c), 20(b)(ii), 25 and 27 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. Briefly stated, it is the case of the prosecution that on 23.08.2019 at about 15.00 hours, accused Nos.3 to 7 were found to be in possession of 45 K.Gs. of 'ganja'. Police have arrested them and seized the contraband from their possession in the presence of mediators. On interrogation, accused No.3 confessed that they are all working under accused No.1, who is running tobacco factory, and on his direction they are selling the 'ganja' in packets to the students of colleges at various places. Therefore, the petitioner, along with other accused, has committed the aforesaid offences.
texts.arguments: Heard learned counsel for the petitioner and learned Sri V.Farooq, learned Assistant Government Pleader representing the learned Additional Public Prosecutor for respondent-State. Learned counsel for the petitioner would contend that the offences under Sections 272, 273 and 328 of IPC are not CMR, J. attracted on the facts of the present case and at best they are only the offences under Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 2003 (for short the "COTP Act") and police cannot register cases in respect of the aforesaid offences under the Indian Penal Code. In support of his contention, he relied on an order passed by this Badam Sampath Kumar vs The State Of Andhra Pradesh on 11 November, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117782937/ 1 Court in Crl.P.No.13783 of 2018 dated 04.01.2019 wherein this Court held that the offences falling within the purview of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the COTP Act cannot be registered for the offences under the Indian Penal Code. He would further contend that as per the judgment of the Apex Court in Lalitha Kumari v. Government of U.P.1 that it is only after making General Diary entry that the police can proceed with the investigation in the case. In this case, eventhough the alleged offence took place at about 15.00 hours that the police made a G.D. entry at 19.00 hours and it is a violation of the directions of the Apex Court issued in Lalitha Kumari1. He would also further contend that the contraband seized in this case cannot be termed as 'ganja' in view of the judgment of the Karnataka High Court (Dharwad Circuit Bench) in K.K. Rejji v. State by Murdeshwar Police Station2. He would also contend that the alleged confession of accused No.3, who is the co-accused, on the basis of which (2014) 2 SCC 1 2010 (95) AIC 765 : 2011 (1) Crimes 508 : 2011 (6) R.C.R. (Cri) 1706 CMR, J. accused No.1 is shown as accused in this case is not valid under law. Therefore, he prayed for grant of anticipatory bail to the petitioner. Sri V. Farooq, learned Assistant Government Pleader representing the learned Additional Public Prosecutor for respondent-State, opposed the anticipatory bail application. He would contend that the information was received by the police at about 19.00 hours and immediately a G.D. entry was also made at 19.00 hours and there is no violation of the directions of the Apex Court. He would further contend that the contraband that was seized from the possession of the accused in this case is 'ganja' and it cannot be held at this stage without the chemical analyst report that it is not a 'ganja' as defined under the Act. Therefore, he prayed for dismissal of the criminal petition. Perused the record. The contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner that the petitioner, who is accused No.1, has been implicated in this case only on the basis of the confessional statement of accused No.3 and that it is not valid, cannot be CMR, J. countenanced. It is relevant to note Section 30 of the Evidence Act, 1872, which reads as follows: "30. Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence.--When more persons than one are being tried jointly for the same offence, and a confession made by one of such persons affecting himself and some other of such persons is proved, the Court may take into consideration such confession as against such other person as well as against the person who makes such confession." Ultimately, if the said confession of the co-accused is proved to Badam Sampath Kumar vs The State Of Andhra Pradesh on 11 November, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117782937/ 2 be true, the same can be acted upon by the Court in the final adjudication of the case.
